a: Then Eliphaz the Temanite spoke up:
p: Eliphaz opens the third and last cycle of speeches. It is the only round where the pattern breaks down.
b: The debate has run in two full rounds: Eliphaz, Job, Bildad, Job, Zophar, Job (chapters 4–14 and 15–21). The third round starts the same way, but it does not finish. Bildad's speech is only five verses (25:2–6), Zophar never speaks, and in two places Job seems to argue his friends' side (24:18–24; 27:13–23). Scholars explain this in three main ways: the text was damaged and later put back together in the wrong order; Job is quoting or mocking his friends; or the author broke the pattern on purpose to show the friends running out of words. The chapter page for chapter 22 sets out each view in full.

a: Can a human being be of any use to God?
t: Does God need anyone to be good?
p: Eliphaz argues that God gains nothing from human goodness, so he has no reason to punish Job without cause.
b: Eliphaz's logic runs this way: God is not helped by a person's righteousness, so he has no motive to treat a righteous man harshly. If Job suffers, it cannot be for his piety (22:4); it must be for his sins (22:5). The argument sounds humble, but it makes God distant: he watches human conduct the way a judge watches a case in which he has no stake. Elihu will make almost the same point (35:6–8). The prologue says the opposite: God does take pleasure in Job (1:8; 2:3), and Job's faithfulness is the very thing at stake in the heavenly wager.

a: Is it because you fear him that he corrects you
p: "Fear" here is Job's reverence for God, the same word Eliphaz used for Job's piety in 4:6.
b: The Hebrew yir'ah is the "fear of God" that marks a faithful life (1:1; 28:28). In 4:6 Eliphaz asked whether Job's "fear of God" should not be what he leans on, meaning Job's piety. Here he turns the word with sarcasm: surely God is not punishing Job for being devout. The verb "corrects" (yakach) and the phrase "takes you to court" (literally "goes with you into judgment") are legal words. Job has been asking for a trial (13:3, 18–22); Eliphaz says Job already has one, and he is losing it.

a: For you held your brothers' goods in pledge for nothing
p: Eliphaz now accuses Job of specific crimes against the poor. Nothing in the book supports these charges.
b: Until now the friends hinted that Job must have sinned. Here Eliphaz names sins: taking pledges without cause, leaving the naked unclothed, refusing water and bread, sending widows away. These are the classic crimes of the rich in Israel's law and prophets (Exodus 22:26–27; Deuteronomy 24:10–13, 17; Amos 2:8). Eliphaz has no evidence; he reasons backward from Job's suffering to the sins that must have caused it. Job will answer each charge point by point (29:12–17; 31:16–22). Readers who know the prologue know Eliphaz is wrong (1:1, 8), and God says so at the end (42:7). Gregory the Great saw Eliphaz as the type of the person who judges by outward results.

a: A man of muscle: the land was his.
p: Literally "man of arm" and "lifted of face": the powerful and the favored. It may describe Job himself.
b: The verse breaks the run of "you" with a third person. Many interpreters read it as a sneer at Job: you were the strongman who owned the land and the favored man who lived on it, so you could get away with abuse. Others take it as a general statement that the powerful seize the land while the weak are crushed (22:9), or as the thought of the oppressor himself. "Lifted of face" (nesu panim) is the idiom for a person whom others show favor or bias toward, as in Isaiah 3:3 and Isaiah 9:15. Some move the verse after 22:9 or treat it as a gloss.
orig: אִישׁ זְרוֹעַ (ish zero'a), "man of arm"; נְשׂוּא פָנִים (nesu panim), "one whose face is lifted"

a: Widows you turned away with empty hands
p: Israel's law names the widow and the fatherless as people God himself protects.
b: The law says, "Never treat a widow or a fatherless child harshly. If you do treat him harshly, and he cries out to me, be sure I will hear his cry" (Exodus 22:22–23). Deuteronomy commands that justice not be bent for the fatherless and that a widow's garment not be taken as a pledge (Deuteronomy 24:17). To accuse Job of crushing the arms of the fatherless is to accuse him of the very sins that call down God's anger in the law. Job's answer is that he was a father to the fatherless and made the widow's heart sing (29:12–13; 31:16–18).

a: or a darkness you cannot see through
p: Darkness and deep water are two more pictures of sudden ruin. The Greek reads the line differently; see the variant panel.
b: The images echo earlier speeches. Job said God holds back the waters or lets them loose to overturn the earth (12:15), and Bildad pictured the wicked man thrust from light into darkness (18:18). Eliphaz now turns both pictures on Job: the dread of 22:10 comes on him like a darkness he cannot see through and a flood that closes over his head.

a: What does God know?
p: Eliphaz claims Job thinks God is too far off to see. Job has said nearly the opposite.
b: Eliphaz pictures Job as a man who says God sits above the clouds and cannot see what happens below (22:13–14). That is the creed of the practical atheist in the Psalms (Psalm 10:11; Psalm 73:11; Psalm 94:7). But Job's complaint has been that God sees him all too well and will not leave him alone (7:17–20; 10:4–7; 14:3). Job does say that God lets the wicked prosper (21:7–16), and Eliphaz may be twisting that. The "rim of the sky" (literally "the circle of heaven") is the dome of the heavens as the ancients pictured it, resting on the horizon (Isaiah 40:22; Proverbs 8:27).

a: a river poured over their foundations
p: Many readers hear in the "old road" of the wicked and the river that swept them away a memory of Noah's Flood.
b: Eliphaz points to an ancient road walked by wicked men who were snatched away before their time, their foundations washed out by a river (22:15–16). Many readers hear the Flood here. Rashi says the river poured into their foundations was the Flood, or the fire and brimstone of Sodom. The Aramaic Targum of Job keeps the picture of a river: they were cut off from the earth before their time, and their body was poured out at the bottom of the river. The Talmud applies the verse differently, to 974 generations that were to have been created before the world and were "snatched away" (Chagigah 13b–14a); it does read Job's own words in 21:14 ("Go away from us") of the Flood generation (Sanhedrin 108a). Many modern commentators agree that the Flood, or a flood story like it, is in view. If so, Eliphaz says Job stands on the wrong side of the oldest judgment in history.

a: The plans of the wicked are far from me!
p: This line repeats Job's own words from 21:16, word for word in Hebrew.
b: In 21:16 Job said the same thing as he described the wicked who prosper and tell God to leave them alone (21:14–15). Eliphaz now repeats Job's phrases, "Go away from us" (22:17; 21:14) and "the plans of the wicked are far from me" (22:18; 21:16), and turns them back on him. The repetition shows that speakers in Job quote each other, sometimes to mock. That habit matters for the third round, where some scholars think Job quotes his friends in turn (24:18–24; 27:13–23).

a: Come to terms with him, and be at peace.
p: The verb means to be used to someone, to get on with him. Eliphaz invites Job back into friendship with God.
b: The Hebrew verb sakan (in the form used here) means "to be familiar with, to get along with" (Numbers 22:30; Psalm 139:3). The KJV's "acquaint now thyself with him" catches part of it. Eliphaz's closing appeal (22:21–30) is warm, and it is the best version of the friends' theology: return, receive God's teaching, put away wrong, and God will restore you. Its weakness is its starting point, that Job's suffering proves his guilt. The book's ending gives an irony: Job will be restored, but only after God says the friends were wrong (42:7–10).
orig: הַסְכֶּן־נָא עִמּוֹ (hasken-na immo), "get along, please, with him"

a: Take the law from his mouth
t: Torah: the law from God's mouth
p: The word is torah. The site renders it "law"; on Eliphaz's lips it means God's instruction, not the Law of Moses.
b: The Hebrew word is torah. Across the Bible it means "instruction, teaching" and, for Israel, the Law given through Moses. The site renders torah as "law" throughout, and this is its only use in Job, so the wider sense is given here. Eliphaz is a man of Teman in Edom, not an Israelite, and the book never mentions Sinai, Moses or the covenant with Israel. So he means God's instruction in general, the way a teacher's torah is his teaching in Proverbs (Proverbs 3:1). Still, keeping God's words stored in the heart sounds like Deuteronomy 6:6 and Deuteronomy 11:18, and Israelite readers would have heard the echo.

a: Lay your gold ore in the dust
p: Eliphaz tells Job to treat his gold as dirt. The rare word betser means raw gold or gold ore.
b: Betser is found only here and in 22:25 (and perhaps 36:19), and seems to mean unworked gold. Ophir was a distant land famous for fine gold, reached by Solomon's ships (1 Kings 9:28; 1 Kings 10:11); its site is unknown, with Arabia, East Africa and India all proposed. Eliphaz's point is that if Job throws away his trust in wealth, God himself will be his treasure (22:25). The line is ironic, since Job has already lost everything he owned. Job will swear he never put his trust in gold (31:24–25).

a: your silver piled high
p: The word to'aphot is rare. It may mean heaps, bars, or peaks; in Numbers it describes the strength of a wild ox.
b: To'aphot occurs only four times. In Numbers 23:22 and Numbers 24:8 it is the "horns" or "strength" of a wild ox; in Psalm 95:4 it is the "peaks" of the mountains. Here translators guess from the context: "choicest," "in heaps," "in bars" or "precious." The Plain takes the picture of silver piled high like mountain peaks. The Greek reads quite differently: "the Almighty will be your helper against enemies, and he will give you back pure, like silver tried in fire."

a: When men are thrown down and you say, 'Up!'
p: The Hebrew is very compressed. It may mean Job will pray for the fallen, or that pride brings people down.
b: Word by word the verse reads: "when they make low, and you say, 'pride' (or 'up'), and the low of eyes he will save." The word gevah can mean "up!" or "pride." Some read: "when they are brought low, you will say, 'It is pride,' and God will save the humble" (compare Proverbs 29:23). Others read it as Job's future prayer: when others fall, Job will say "Lift them up," and God will save them. That second reading fits 22:30, where Job's clean hands rescue others. The Greek reads "because he humbled him, and you will say, 'He acted proudly,'" which supports "pride."

a: He will set free a man who is guilty
p: Eliphaz says a clean-handed man's prayer can save the guilty. At the end, Job prays and the friends are spared.
b: The Hebrew i-naqi means "not innocent": i is a rare negative, as in the name Ichabod, "no glory" (1 Samuel 4:21). The KJV read i as "island" ("the island of the innocent"), a likely mistranslation. Many modern scholars emend to ish naqi, "the innocent man," which gives a smoother line, "he will rescue the innocent," and several translations adopt it. Read as it stands, Eliphaz means that if Job repents, his purity will be strong enough to rescue even sinners. The irony is deep. In 42:7–9 God tells Eliphaz that he and his friends did not speak rightly, and that Job will pray for them; God accepts Job's prayer and spares them. Eliphaz himself becomes the guilty man saved by Job's clean hands, an irony that commentators such as Andersen and Habel point out.

a: Still today my complaint is defiant
p: The Hebrew meri means "rebellion." Ancient versions read mar, "bitter."
b: The Masoretic Text has meri, "rebellion, defiance," as if Job admits his complaint sounds rebellious to his friends, or insists on it. The Syriac, the Targum and the Latin Vulgate read mar, "bitter," the word Job used in 7:11 and 10:1, and many English versions follow them. The Plain keeps the Hebrew because it is the harder reading and makes sense: Job will not tone down his protest. Job does not answer Eliphaz's charges directly in this speech. He speaks past him, about God.
orig: מְרִי שִׂחִי (meri sichi), "rebellion is my complaint"

a: Would that someone could tell me how to find him
p: Eliphaz told Job to return to God (22:23). Job answers that he would, if only he could find him.
b: The cry "Who will give that I knew" is a Hebrew way of saying "If only." Job wants to reach God's "seat" (tekhunah, a fixed place or dwelling) and argue his case there (23:4–7). He is sure that in a fair hearing an upright man would win. This is a bolder hope than in 9:32–35, where Job feared God would crush him in court and wished for an umpire between them. The search in 23:8–9 then fails in every direction. Christian readers have heard here the soul's search for a hidden God (Gregory the Great; Calvin's sermons), and Jewish readers the problem of God's hiddenness, hester panim.

a: and I would walk free from my judge forever
p: Job pictures leaving court acquitted. The Greek and the Vulgate read "my case" for "my judge."
b: The Hebrew va'afalletah lanetsach mishshofti means "I would escape forever from my judge," that is, walk out of court free of the charge. The Old Greek has "may he bring my judgment (to krima mou) to an end," and the Vulgate "may my case (judicium meum) come to victory"; both point to mishpati, "my case," which some scholars adopt. The Aramaic Targum from Qumran (11QtgJob) survives for parts of 23:1–8; at 23:7 it has a phrase rendered "for truth and law," which, like the Greek's "truth and reproof" in the first line, differs from the Masoretic wording (Zuckerman and Reed; the official edition, DJD 23, was not consulted). Either way, Job is confident that a fair trial would clear him. "Upright" (yashar) is one of the words God used of Job in the prologue (1:1, 8).

a: Look: I walk ahead, and he is missing
p: Forward, back, left and right are also Hebrew words for east, west, north and south.
b: A Hebrew speaker faced east to take his bearings. So qedem, "front," is also "east"; achor, "back," is "west"; semol, "left," is "north"; and yamin, "right," is "south" (hence Yemen, "the south"). Job searches every point of the compass and finds no God. The passage is a dark mirror of Psalm 139:7–10, where the psalmist cannot escape God in any direction. Job's problem is the opposite: he cannot reach him.
orig: קֶדֶם... אָחוֹר... שְׂמֹאול... יָמִין (qedem, achor, semol, yamin)

a: Once he has assayed me, I will come out like gold.
p: Job is sure that once God has put him through the fire, like gold in a refiner's furnace, he will come out pure.
b: Refining gold meant melting it so the waste could be skimmed off. Scripture often uses the picture for God testing his people (Psalm 66:10; Proverbs 17:3; Zechariah 13:9; Malachi 3:3). Job uses it as a claim of innocence: there is no waste in me to burn off. Christian readers later took the verse as a picture of suffering that purifies faith, as in 1 Peter 1:7, and it is one of the most quoted lines in Job. In context it is a lawsuit statement, not yet a comfort: Job wants the test so that he can be cleared. The verb is a perfect, "he has tested me": Job speaks of the test as already under way, or as certain to end well.
r: Psalm 66:10; Proverbs 17:3; Zechariah 13:9; Malachi 3:3; 1 Peter 1:7; Wisdom of Solomon 3:5–6

a: more than my own portion
p: "My portion" is probably Job's daily food. The Greek reads "in my bosom"; see the variant panel.
b: The Masoretic mechuqqi, "more than my portion," uses the word for an allotted share, as in Proverbs 30:8, "my portion of bread." Job claims that God's words mattered more to him than his food, a thought close to Deuteronomy 8:3 and to Jesus' answer in Matthew 4:4.

a: But he is one, and who can make him turn?
p: The Hebrew is strange: "he is in one." It may mean God is unique, or that his mind is made up.
b: Literally "and he in one." Some take be as "as" and read "he is one," echoing Deuteronomy 6:4 in a dark key: the one God answers to no one. Others read "he is of one mind," so no plea can change him (KJV). A few scholars emend to bachar, "he has chosen." All readings agree on the point: God does what he wants (23:13b), and Job's terror comes from this (23:15–16), not from guilt.
orig: וְהוּא בְאֶחָד (vehu ve'echad), "and he in one"

a: For it is not the darkness that has undone me
p: The verse can be read three ways. It is one of the hardest lines in a hard chapter.
b: Word by word: "for not I am destroyed (or silenced) from before darkness, and from before me gloom covers." One reading: "I am not silenced by the darkness," so Job keeps speaking in spite of it. Another takes the "not" with a wish: "If only I had been cut off before the darkness came" (compare 3:11–16). A third deletes "not" and reads "I am undone by the darkness." The Plain keeps the negative: the darkness has not finished Job off. What terrifies him is God, not the gloom (23:16).

a: Why has the Almighty laid up no set times?
t: Why does God keep no court days?
p: Job asks why God sets no days for judgment, so that the faithful can see justice done.
b: "Times" and "his days" are times of reckoning, like court days on which a ruler hears cases (compare "the day of the LORD," Amos 5:18; Isaiah 2:12). Job's complaint is wider than his own case: the whole world runs without visible justice. Chapter 24 is Job's fullest look at the suffering of other people, the poor who are robbed and work the rich man's fields hungry (24:2–12). Ketiv and Qere differ on one word here ("those who know him," plural, in the reading tradition; "he who knows him" in the written text), with no change in sense.
orig: מַדּוּעַ מִשַּׁדַּי לֹא־נִצְפְּנוּ עִתִּים (maddua mishShaddai lo-nitsp'nu ittim)

a: Men nudge the boundary stones along
p: Moving a neighbor's boundary stone was a grave crime in Israel's law and in the wider ancient world.
b: In a farming world, land was life, and its edges were marked with stones. Deuteronomy forbids moving them (Deuteronomy 19:14), and the curse ceremony includes, "A curse on anyone who shifts his neighbor's boundary marker!" (Deuteronomy 27:17). Proverbs warns not to move "the ancient boundary" or to enter "the fields of the fatherless" (Proverbs 22:28; Proverbs 23:10). Babylonian boundary stones (kudurru) carried curses on anyone who moved them, and the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope (about 1100 BC) has a whole chapter on it. Job lists the crime first among the deeds that God seems to ignore.

a: the widow's ox they keep as security
p: Lenders took animals or tools as security for loans. The law limited what could be taken from the poor.
b: A pledge was something the borrower handed over until the loan was repaid. The law forbade taking a millstone, "for that would be taking a life as a pledge," and required a poor man's coat to be returned by night (Deuteronomy 24:6, 12–13). Taking the widow's only ox, or the orphan's only donkey, left them no way to farm or carry loads. Job's list (24:2–4) reads like a list of violations of these laws, though the book never cites the law of Moses by name. Eliphaz accused Job of this very sin (22:6); Job says the wicked do it, and God lets them.

a: wild donkeys in the wilderness
p: The poor are driven out to scavenge in the desert like wild animals.
b: The wild donkey or onager lived in the desert and was a picture of a creature beyond human control (Genesis 16:12; 39:5–8). Here it pictures people pushed to the edge of the settled land, forced to forage in the scrub for something to feed their children. The same outcasts seem to reappear in 30:3–8, where Job describes the desert-dwellers who now mock him. Some readers see one group in both passages; others, that Job's sympathy in chapter 24 turns to contempt in chapter 30.

a: Out in the field they cut fodder
p: The Hebrew belilo, "his fodder," can also be split as beli lo, "not his," a field that is not theirs.
b: The written consonants blylw can be read as belilo, "his mixed fodder" (as in 6:5), or divided as beli lo, "not his own." The second gives "they reap in a field that is not theirs," which matches the parallel "the wicked man's vineyard." The Greek has "a field not their own." Either way, the poor do the harvest work for the rich and keep none of it. The Ketiv and Qere differ on the verb ("they make others reap" or "they reap") with little change in sense.

a: Others pull a fatherless baby from the breast
p: This verse breaks the description of the desert poor with a return to their oppressors. Some move it after 24:3.
b: Verses 5–8 and 10–12 describe the poor; verse 9 suddenly speaks of the oppressors again, who seize a nursing child for a debt. Many scholars think the verse belongs after 24:3, where the oppressors are listed, and some translations move it. Others think the shift is natural in poetry: the poor are poor because their children are taken. The second line, "they take a pledge from the poor," may be repointed to "they take the infant of the poor in pledge" ('ul, "infant," for 'al, "on"). Seizing children for debt is attested in 2 Kings 4:1 and Nehemiah 5:5.

a: yet God takes no notice of the wrong
p: Literally "God does not set offensiveness": he does not count it as a wrong. The Syriac reads differently; see the variant panel.
b: The Hebrew tiflah means something unseemly or offensive (1:22 uses the same word: Job did not charge God with anything "unfitting"). "God does not set tiflah" means he does not treat it as a wrong, or does not charge anyone with it. It is the boldest line of the chapter: Job says outright that God ignores the cries of the dying. The Masoretic Text also reads "men" (metim, מְתִים), where with other vowels the word is "the dying" (metim, מֵתִים), a reading many scholars prefer.

a: These are among the rebels against the light.
p: The murderer, the adulterer and the burglar work by night. Light here is both daylight and moral light.
b: Verses 13–17 describe three night-workers: the murderer who rises before dawn, the adulterer who waits for dusk, the burglar who digs through mud-brick walls in the dark. They "rebel against the light": daylight exposes them, so morning is to them what midnight is to others (24:17). The picture is close to John 3:19–20, where people love darkness because their deeds are evil, and to Proverbs 7:9 on the adulterer at twilight. The lines also answer Eliphaz, who said God cannot see through the clouds (22:13–14): the wicked count on the dark.

a: In the dark one digs through into houses
p: Most houses were built of mud brick, and thieves dug through the walls rather than break the door.
b: The verb chatar means "to dig through," the same word used of a thief caught tunneling in Exodus 22:2, where the law treats a night burglary differently from a daytime one. Jesus uses the picture of the thief who "digs through" (Matthew 6:19–20; Matthew 24:43). Mud-brick walls made this easier than breaking a guarded door. The detail shows that Job's world, though set in Uz, is the ordinary world of village Israel.

a: He is carried off, light, across the waters
t: Is Job arguing his friends' side?
p: In 24:18–24 Job seems to say the wicked come to a quick end, the very thing he has denied. Readers explain it in several ways.
b: Job has argued that the wicked prosper (21:7–33) and that God ignores their crimes (24:1–12). Now the wicked are carried off on the water, their land is cursed, and Sheol takes them. 1. Misplaced speech. Many scholars give 24:18–24 to a lost speech of Zophar (Pope, Dhorme) or of Bildad, displaced when the third round was damaged. 2. Quotation. Others hear Job quoting the friends; the RSV and ESV add "You say," which the Hebrew does not have (compare Gordis). 3. Job's own wish or view. Or Job curses the wicked ("let their portion be cursed"), or grants that they do die, but late and like everyone else (24:24). The witnesses. No manuscript puts these verses anywhere else. The Old Greek lacked 24:14b–18a (Origen filled the gap from Theodotion), and its 24:18b–24 is a curse, "May their earthly portion be cursed" (checked in NETS). The Qumran Targum has a gap at 24:18–23 (Zuckerman and Reed). The Talmud reads 24:18 of the Flood generation, swept off on the waters (Sanhedrin 108a). The Plain keeps the Hebrew order.

a: so is the sinner by Sheol
p: Sheol is the Hebrew name for the world of the dead, where all go, good and bad. It is not the same as hell.
b: In Job, Sheol is a shadowy place under the earth, a land of darkness (10:21–22) where the dead lie still. Everyone goes there (3:13–19; 30:23). Here the point is how fast it takes the sinner: as summer heat dries up the water from melted snow, Sheol swallows the wicked. The KJV renders Sheol as "the grave" here and "hell" elsewhere, which can mislead, since the idea of a place of punishment for the wicked developed later. See the Sheol topic.

a: the maggot sucks at him
p: Literally "the maggot sucks him sweetly." The grave reverses the rich man's feasting.
b: The verb mataq means "to be sweet." The wicked man who found evil sweet in his mouth (20:12, in Zophar's speech) is now sweet food for maggots. The womb that bore him forgets him, so his name dies too, which for an Israelite was the deepest loss (18:17; Psalm 109:13). The last line, "wrong is snapped off like a tree," contrasts with Job's own image of a tree that sprouts again after it is cut down (14:7–9). Bildad made the same comparison of humans and maggots (25:6).

a: Yet by his power he hauls away the strong
p: The subject is just "he." It may be God, who brings the strong down, or the wicked man, who drags others off.
b: The Hebrew has no noun. Read with 24:23 ("his eyes are on their ways"), "he" is God, who lets the wicked feel secure but watches them and brings them down. Read with 24:21, "he" is the wicked man, who drags off the strong and rises up while no one is sure of his life. The second half is also open: "they have no hope of life" or "he rises when he has no hope of life." Many translations add "God" to settle it. The Plain keeps "he."

a: Then Bildad the Shuhite spoke up:
t: Why is Bildad's speech so short?
p: Bildad's third speech is only five verses. Zophar, who should speak next, never does.
b: Every earlier speech by a friend ran at least 20 verses. This one has five verses of speech (25:2–6), and the Old Greek lacked even part of that: 25:6b was filled in from Theodotion (NETS; Gentry). Some scholars think the rest of Bildad's speech survives in 26:5–14, which sounds like a friend's hymn to God's power and follows naturally on 25:6 (Dhorme, Pope, Clines and many others). Others read the shortness as the point: the friends have run out of arguments, and Bildad can only repeat a line Eliphaz has already used twice (4:17–19; 15:14–16). Job then cuts him off (26:2). The silence of Zophar is read the same two ways: lost, or deliberately absent. See the chapter page.

a: in his heights he makes peace
p: This line passed into Jewish prayer: "He who makes peace in his heights" closes the Kaddish and the Amidah.
b: The phrase oseh shalom bimromav is quoted in the closing line of the Kaddish, the prayer of praise said in the synagogue and by mourners, and at the end of the Amidah, the central standing prayer: "He who makes peace in his heights, may he make peace for us." Bildad means that God imposes order on the heavens, perhaps after conflict among heavenly powers or stars (compare Isaiah 24:21; Revelation 12:7). The rabbis read it as God making peace between the angels of fire and water (Rashi on this verse).

a: How then can a mortal be in the right with God?
t: Job's question, turned back on him
p: Job asked this question, in the same Hebrew words, in 9:2. Bildad now uses it to say no one, Job included, can be pure.
b: Job asked, "how can a mortal be in the right with God?" (9:2), meaning that God is too strong to face in court. Bildad takes the same words to mean that no human is morally clean enough to stand before God. The idea that no one born of a woman is pure first came to Eliphaz in a night vision (4:17) and he repeated it (15:14). Paul draws on the same conviction in a different direction: all have sinned (Romans 3:23), so righteousness must come as a gift. The friends use it only to silence Job.

a: how much less a human, a maggot
p: Bildad calls humans rimmah, "maggot," and tole'ah, "worm." Psalm 22:6 uses the second word of the sufferer.
b: Both words are for the grubs that feed on rotting things (24:20; Exodus 16:20). Bildad's conclusion is that humans are too lowly to complain. The second line, "a son of man, a worm," uses ben adam, "son of a human," a common Hebrew phrase for "a mortal" (Psalm 8:4; Ezekiel 2:1). The Plain gives "a mortal." The same word tole'ah appears in the psalm cry "I am a worm and not a man" (Psalm 22:6), which the Gospels set at the cross. Christian readers sometimes contrast the friend who uses the word to crush the sufferer with the psalmist who uses it of himself.

a: What a help you have been to the powerless!
p: The "you" in 26:2–4 is singular. Job is mocking one friend, most likely Bildad.
b: In most of his speeches Job addresses the friends together with plural "you." Here the verbs are singular, so he is answering the last speaker, Bildad (or, if the order has been disturbed, whichever friend spoke last). The lines are sarcasm: what a help you have been to me, the weak one, and what wisdom you have shown me, the fool. "Whose breath" (26:4) may hint that Bildad's words came from someone else, Eliphaz, whose line he repeated (25:4; 4:17).

a: The shades writhe
t: The Rephaim, the shades of the dead
p: The Rephaim are the dead in the underworld. Elsewhere the same word names an ancient race of giants.
b: Repha'im means the dead, the faint "shades" who dwell in Sheol (Psalm 88:10; Proverbs 9:18; Isaiah 14:9; Isaiah 26:14). At Ugarit, the rpum were the honored dead, royal ancestors. In Deuteronomy and Joshua, Rephaim are also a tall people of ancient Canaan (Deuteronomy 2:11; Deuteronomy 3:11). The Greek here reads "giants" (gigantes). "Below the waters" places the dead under the cosmic sea beneath the earth. Even there, the dead tremble before God.
r: Psalm 88:10; Proverbs 9:18; Isaiah 14:9; Isaiah 26:14; Deuteronomy 2:11; Deuteronomy 3:11

a: below the waters and those who live in them.
p: Many scholars give this hymn to Bildad, as the lost rest of chapter 25. Others keep it as Job's.
b: The hymn to God's power over the dead, the sky and the sea fits Bildad's theme in 25:2–6, and his speech is otherwise too short. Dhorme, Pope, Clines and the New American Bible (1970) are among those who join 25:1–6 and 26:5–14. Against this, Job has praised God's power in similar words before (9:5–10; 12:13–25), and the hymn's end, "these are the mere edges of his ways" (26:14), fits Job's sense that God is beyond understanding. The Old Greek lacked 26:5–11 and 26:14a, so its hymn had only 26:12–13 and 26:14b; Origen supplied the rest from Theodotion (checked in NETS). The Qumran Targum keeps parts of 26:10–27:4 in the Hebrew order (Zuckerman and Reed). Habel and others read 26:5–14 as Job outdoing Bildad at his own game: you speak of God's greatness? Let me show you how great he is.

a: there is no cover over Abaddon
p: Abaddon means "Destruction," another name for the world of the dead. In Revelation it becomes the name of an angel.
b: Abaddon comes from the verb avad, "perish." In the poetry of the Hebrew Bible it stands beside Sheol and Death as a name for the underworld (28:22; 31:12; Psalm 88:11; Proverbs 15:11). Proverbs 15:11 makes the same point as Job here: Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD, so how much more human hearts. In Revelation 9:11 Abaddon is the name of the angel of the abyss, in Greek Apollyon.

a: Over the empty waste he spreads the north
t: Zaphon and an earth hung on nothing
p: "The north" is Zaphon, the mountain of the gods in Canaanite myth. Some read the verse as early cosmology.
b: Tsafon is "north," but also Mount Zaphon (Jebel Aqra in Syria), home of Baal in the Ugaritic myths (compare Psalm 48:2; Isaiah 14:13). Here it may mean the northern sky, spread like a tent over tohu, the "empty waste" of Genesis 1:2. "He hangs the earth on nothing" (belimah, "no-thing") is striking, since most ancient pictures set the earth on pillars (9:6; 38:6). Some modern readers see an anticipation of the earth floating in space; most commentators read it as poetry about God's power: nothing holds the world up but him.

a: He screens off the sight of his throne
p: The Hebrew kisse, "throne," may be a spelling of keseh, "full moon," as in Psalm 81:3.
b: The Masoretic Text has kisse', "throne," with a rare spelling. Many scholars read keseh, "full moon" (Psalm 81:3; Proverbs 7:20), which fits the clouds and the circle of light and dark in 26:8–10. The Plain keeps "throne": God hides his seat in the sky behind clouds, as in Psalm 97:2, "Cloud and dense darkness are all around him." The two readings differ only in a letter.

a: he struck Rahab down
p: Job uses the ancient picture of God defeating the sea monster. The verse has close parallels in the texts from Ugarit.
b: In Canaanite myth Baal defeats Yam, the Sea, and the monster Lotan, "the fleeing serpent" (btn brh), the same phrase as nachash bariach in 26:13 ("the fleeing snake") and Isaiah 27:1. In the Babylonian Enuma Elish, Marduk splits the sea monster Tiamat. The Bible uses the same imagery for the LORD's power over chaos: Rahab and the sea (9:13; Psalm 89:10; Isaiah 51:9). The verb raga' can mean "stir up" or "still"; the Plain gives "quelled." Most scholars hold that the Bible borrows the myth's images while denying that any rival power is real; the Greek already turns Rahab into a sea creature (ketos).

a: Look, these are the mere edges of his ways
p: All these wonders are just the fringe of God's works, a faint whisper of him. The thunder of his full power no one can grasp.
b: The "edges" (qetsot) are the outer ends, like the hem of a robe. The "whisper of a word" (shemets davar) is a faint sound, the same rare noun Eliphaz used for the word that reached his ear in a vision (4:12, where the site renders it "murmur"). The verse anticipates the speeches from the storm (38–41), where God shows Job the wonders of creation, and Job's final words, that he had only heard about God (42:5). Christian and Jewish mystics alike quoted the verse on the limits of human knowledge of God. The Qere reads "his ways" and "his mighty deeds" in the plural; the Ketiv has the singular.
orig: קְצוֹת דְּרָכָו (qetsot derakhav), "the ends of his ways"; שֵׁמֶץ דָּבָר (shemets davar), "a whisper of a word"

a: Job took up his poem again and said:
p: Instead of "Job spoke up," the text says Job "took up his mashal," his poem or discourse.
b: Every speech so far began "then X spoke up" (literally "answered"). Here and at 29:1 the formula changes: Job "added to lift up his mashal." A mashal is a proverb, a taunt, a wise poem or a parable; Balaam's oracles are introduced the same way (Numbers 23:7, 18). The new formula, with no friend having spoken in between, is one reason many think something is missing here, perhaps Zophar's third speech. Others see a deliberate shift: Job is no longer answering the friends, but making his closing speech.
orig: וַיֹּסֶף אִיּוֹב שְׂאֵת מְשָׁלוֹ (vayyosef Iyyov se'et meshalo)

a: By the life of God, who has stripped me of my right
t: Swearing by the God who wronged him
p: Job takes an oath by God's life, and in the same breath says that God has taken away his rights.
b: "As God lives" (chai-el) is the strongest oath an Israelite could take (Judges 8:19; 1 Samuel 14:39; Ruth 3:13). The paradox is sharp: Job appeals to God as the guarantor of truth while charging God with injustice. Mishpat, "justice" or "right," is Job's legal right to a fair verdict. Later readers have felt the tension. Some saw rebellion. Others saw faith, since Job still swears by the God he accuses, and expects him, finally, to be just. The Greek softens it: "who has judged me so."

a: Until the day I die I will not set my integrity aside.
p: Job's integrity (tummah) is the theme word of the prologue: God and Job's wife both speak of it.
b: Tummah, "integrity, wholeness," belongs to the same root as tam, "wholehearted," God's word for Job (1:1, 8). God says Job "still holds on to his integrity" (2:3), and Job's wife asks, "Still holding on to your integrity?" (2:9). Here Job uses the same phrase as his oath: he will not let it go. To agree with the friends that he must have sinned would be a lie, and so a loss of integrity. Job's honesty is his faithfulness. Job will use the word once more in his oath (31:6).

a: Let my enemy share the fate of the wicked
p: Job curses his enemy. He may mean the friends, who have become his accusers.
b: In the legal language of the debate, an "enemy" or "one who rises against me" is the opponent at law. Job has come to treat his friends as accusers (19:21–22). His wish that his accuser be treated as a criminal fits the ancient rule that a false accuser suffers the penalty he sought (Deuteronomy 19:16–19). Some think Job's enemy here is God himself, whom he has called his adversary (16:9; 19:11); but Job would hardly wish the wicked man's fate on God. 27:7–10 may also belong to the lost speech of Zophar in some reconstructions.

a: So why are you breathing out this empty air?
p: A word play: "you breathe out hevel," the vapor or breath that Ecclesiastes uses for "meaningless."
b: Hevel is breath, mist, a puff of air: the word behind Ecclesiastes' "meaningless, meaningless" (Ecclesiastes 1:2). Here it is both noun and verb, "why do you vapor vapor," so the friends' words are nothing but breath. The "you" is now plural: Job turns to all three friends. Job has called their words wind before (16:3) and their comfort empty (21:34).

a: This is the share a wicked person has with God
p: 27:13–23 describes the doom of the wicked in the friends' terms. Its first line nearly repeats Zophar's last line (20:29).
b: Zophar ended his second speech: this is the wicked man's portion from God (20:29). Here, with only small changes, the same line opens a poem in which the wicked man's children die, his wealth goes to the righteous, and the east wind blows him away. Job has argued the opposite (21:7–33). The Old Greek lacked 27:19b and 27:21–23 (checked in NETS). Reconstruction: many scholars (Dhorme, Pope, Clines and others, with variations) assign 27:13–23 to Zophar's missing third speech, sometimes with 27:7–10 and 24:18–24. Quotation or irony: others read it as Job quoting the friends' doctrine back at them, "this is what you say the wicked get" (Gordis), perhaps as a warning that by their own rule false accusers will suffer (27:7). Job's own view: still others think Job, for all his protest, still believes God will finally judge the wicked, which is why he cannot accept being treated as one (Andersen, Hartley).

a: Those he leaves behind will be buried by plague
p: Literally "buried by death." Here, as in Jeremiah, "death" means plague, so no one is left to bury them properly.
b: In Jeremiah 15:2 and Jeremiah 18:21, "death" (mavet) stands beside sword and famine as a name for epidemic disease; the Greek of Revelation 6:8 uses "death" the same way. To be buried by the plague means to die in an epidemic and be thrown into a common grave, without mourning: even his widows do not weep (compare Psalm 78:64). For a man whose name was meant to live on in his family, this was the final curse.

a: like a lean-to a watchman puts together
p: A watchman's shelter was put up in the field for the harvest and left to fall apart.
b: The watchman's hut was a temporary booth put up in a vineyard or melon patch during harvest and left to collapse afterward (Isaiah 1:8; Isaiah 24:20). Like the moth's cocoon in the first line, it is a house that cannot last. On the moth and the spider of the Greek and Syriac, see the variant panel.

a: They clap their hands at him
p: Clapping the hands and hissing were ancient gestures of scorn over a ruined person or city.
b: Passers-by clap and hiss at the ruins of Jerusalem (Lamentations 2:15) and at fallen Edom and Babylon (Jeremiah 49:17; Jeremiah 50:13). The Hebrew of this verse is unclear about who does it: literally "he claps at him their hands, and hisses at him from his place." The subject may be the east wind of 27:21 (as if the storm itself mocks him), God, or simply people in general. The Plain says "they," people in general, which keeps the subject open.

a: For there is a place where silver comes out of the ground
p: No new speaker is named, so the Hebrew gives the poem to Job. Many scholars think it is the narrator's interlude.
b: In the Hebrew, Job is still speaking: the last heading was "Job took up his poem again" (27:1), and the Plain follows that order. But the poem's calm differs from Job's anguish before and after it, and its answer (28:28) seems to settle the debate before God speaks. So many scholars (Westermann, Habel, Newsom) read it as the narrator's interlude. Clines moves it to the end of Elihu's speeches. Others (Andersen, Janzen) keep it as Job's: having rejected the friends' wisdom, Job says true wisdom is beyond everyone, himself included. The first word bears on the question. The poem opens with ki, "for" or "surely," which the Plain keeps as "For." Read as "for," it ties the poem to Job's words in chapter 27; read as "surely," it is an odd way to begin a new poem, and some take it as a sign that the poem was set here from elsewhere. The chapter page sets out the views.

a: and stone is melted down into copper
p: Chapter 28 is the Bible's fullest picture of mining: shafts, tunnels, dams and smelting fires.
b: Copper was mined and smelted in the Arabah south of the Dead Sea, at Timna and at Faynan (biblical Punon), from early times through the Iron Age; Deuteronomy calls Israel a land where "you can dig copper out of its hills" (Deuteronomy 8:9). Egypt mined turquoise and copper in Sinai. Miners sank shafts, cut galleries, lowered themselves on ropes (28:4) and used fire to crack rock (28:5). Gold and silver came mostly from farther lands. The poet chose the most daring human enterprise he knew to make his point: humans can reach the hidden places of the earth, but not wisdom.

a: The miner sets an end to darkness
p: The Hebrew says only "he." Most read it as the human miner; a few think it is God.
b: The verbs in 28:3–11 have no named subject. The Hebrew says only "he," with a plural in 28:4. Most commentators take "he" as the human miner, since 28:4 speaks of being far from people and 28:13 says no human knows wisdom's worth. The Plain names "the miner" in 28:3 and 28:9 and keeps "he" between, so that one subject runs through 28:3–11; the plural of 28:4 becomes "the miners." A few scholars think God is the subject of 28:9–11, since only God overturns mountains (9:5). "Deep darkness" (tsalmavet) is the word the KJV renders "the shadow of death" (Psalm 23:4).
orig: קֵץ שָׂם לַחֹשֶׁךְ (qets sam lachoshekh), "an end he puts to the darkness"

a: the miners hang there, far from humankind, and sway
t: A verse no one is sure of
p: Almost every word of 28:4 is uncertain. The best guess is miners hanging on ropes in deep shafts.
b: Word by word: "he breaks open a channel (or shaft) away from one who sojourns; the forgotten ones from foot; they hang down from humankind, they swing." The KJV took it as floods breaking out. Most moderns see miners lowered on ropes into shafts in places no traveler walks. The Greek takes it as a moral statement: "those who forget the right way have grown weak among mortals." The Plain gives the mining reading and marks the doubt here.

a: the home of the sky-blue gem
p: The Hebrew sappir is probably lapis lazuli, a deep-blue stone flecked with gold, not the modern sapphire.
b: Lapis lazuli was mined in Afghanistan and traded across the ancient Near East; it often has golden flecks of pyrite, which may explain the gold dust of the second line. The true sapphire was hardly known before Roman times. The same word describes the pavement under God's feet (Exodus 24:10) and his throne (Ezekiel 1:26). The Greek sappheiros, and from it the English "sapphire," took the name over. The Plain says "the sky-blue gem" rather than give it a modern name.

a: It is a track the bird of prey has never learned
t: A path no eye has seen
p: Sharp-eyed birds and proud beasts cannot find the miner's path. Even less can anyone find the path to wisdom.
b: Birds of prey were famous for their sight (39:29). Lions and "sons of pride" (great wild animals, as in 41:34) roam where they like. Yet none of them has seen the underground world the miner reaches (28:7–8). The poem builds a ladder: animals cannot find the miner's path, humans can (28:9–11); humans cannot find wisdom's path (28:12–22), God can (28:23). Paul's "what no eye has seen" (1 Corinthians 2:9) draws on Isaiah 64:4, not on Job, but readers have long joined the two.

a: He binds up the rivers so they do not seep
p: Literally he binds rivers "from weeping." Ugaritic shows that the phrase means the sources where rivers trickle out.
b: The Hebrew mibbekhi neharot looks like "from the weeping of rivers." In the Ugaritic myths, El lives "at the sources of the rivers" (mbk nhrm), the same phrase. So the miner stops up the springs that seep into his shafts. The ancient versions guessed: the Greek has "he uncovered the depths of rivers." This is one of many places where texts from Ugarit (discovered in 1929) have helped explain rare words in Job.

a: But wisdom: where can it be found?
p: This question is asked twice (28:12, 20). The answer comes at the end: only God knows the way.
b: The refrain divides the poem: human skill can find metals and gems (28:1–11); wisdom cannot be found anywhere or bought at any price (28:13–22); God alone knows its place (28:23–28). Later Jewish wisdom writers took up the poem. Baruch 3:15, a book in the Catholic and Orthodox Old Testament, asks who has found wisdom's place, and answers that God found the way to her and gave her to Israel as the Law (Baruch 3:29–4:1). Sirach 24 pictures Wisdom settling in Israel, and the Wisdom of Solomon 7–9 describes her as a vapor rising from God's power. In Job she stays hidden.
r: 28:20; 28:23; Proverbs 8:22–31; Baruch 3:15; Baruch 3:29–4:1; Sirach 1:1–10; Sirach 24:1–23; Wisdom of Solomon 7:25–27

a: No human knows what it is worth
p: "Its worth" prepares for the prices in 28:15–19. The Greek reads "its way"; see the variant panel.
b: The Masoretic 'erkah is a price or valuation, the word for the value set on a vow in Leviticus 27:2–8. The poem moves from where wisdom is (28:12) to what it would cost (28:15–19), and back to where it is (28:20–23). Humans know the price of silver and gems; they do not know the price of wisdom, because it is not for sale.

a: 'It is not in me,' says the Deep
t: The Deep and the Sea speak
p: Tehom (the Deep) and Yam (the Sea) are the great waters, which in older myths were gods. Here they are only creatures.
b: Tehom is the "deep" of Genesis 1:2, related to the Babylonian Tiamat; Yam is the Canaanite sea god. Here both are personified but tamed: they speak only to confess that wisdom is not in them, and Abaddon and Death say the same (28:22). The poem walks the whole universe, from the depths to the sky, and finds no wisdom in it. The Hebrew Bible never lets the deep or the sea be divine, but it borrows their old names and voices.

a: nor rare carnelian, nor the sky-blue gem
t: Gems no one can name for sure
p: Ancient gem names are hard to match with modern stones. Carnelian, coral, crystal and topaz are educated guesses.
b: Shoham (28:16) is one of the stones of Eden (Genesis 2:12) and of the high priest's ephod (Exodus 28:9); "onyx" or "carnelian" are guesses. Ra'mot and gavish (28:18) are perhaps coral and rock crystal. Peninim may be pearls, red coral or rubies (Proverbs 3:15; Lamentations 4:7). Pitdah of Cush (28:19) is "topaz" in the Greek tradition, perhaps peridot from an island in the Red Sea. The Plain uses "carnelian" for shoham and "the sky-blue gem" for sappir (see 28:6), and lets the list do its work: wisdom outranks every treasure.
r: Genesis 2:12; Exodus 28:9; Exodus 28:17–20; Proverbs 3:13–15; Proverbs 8:11; Revelation 21:19–20

a: Abaddon and Death say
t: Even Death has only heard of it
p: The realm of the dead, which knows all secrets of the deep, has heard only a rumor of wisdom.
b: Abaddon ("Destruction") and Death are paired as names of the underworld, as in 26:6 and Proverbs 15:11. In 26:6 Sheol and Abaddon lie naked before God; here they confess their own ignorance. The upward and downward search ends: the living cannot see it (28:21), the dead have only heard of it (28:22). Only the Creator knows (28:23).

a: God has the insight into its road
p: God knows where wisdom is because he used it when he made the world.
b: The poem's turn: God, who sees the ends of the earth, saw wisdom, weighed its worth and set it in place when he fixed the weight of the wind and the paths of rain and thunder (28:24–27). This is close to Proverbs 8:22–31, where Wisdom is beside God at creation, and Proverbs 3:19, which says the LORD laid the earth's foundations by wisdom. Christian writers later read such passages in light of Christ as the Wisdom and Word of God (1 Corinthians 1:24; John 1:1–3; Colossians 1:15–17), though Job 28 itself pictures wisdom as something God sees and sets, not a person beside him.
r: Proverbs 3:19; Proverbs 8:22–31; Psalm 104:24; Jeremiah 10:12; 1 Corinthians 1:24; Colossians 1:15–17; John 1:1–3

a: and a road for the thundercloud
t: Rain and thunder: a preview of the storm
p: These lines anticipate God's speech from the storm, which asks who opens a road for the thundercloud (38:25).
b: The phrase "a road for the thundercloud" (derekh lachaziz qolot) returns word for word in God's speech (38:25), and the site renders it the same way in both places. The rain's "law" (choq, a decree or fixed limit) recalls the boundaries God sets for the sea (38:10). Whoever placed this poem here prepared the reader for chapters 38–39: the order of creation shows God's wisdom, which humans cannot master.

a: the fear of the Lord is wisdom
t: "The Lord": Adonai, only here in Job
p: This is the only place in Job where God is called Adonai, "the Lord." It is a different word from the LORD, YHWH.
b: The poet and the speakers in Job avoid Israel's divine name YHWH ("the LORD") in the debate, except once (12:9, "the LORD's hand"), using El, Eloah and Shaddai. Here the text has Adonai, "the Lord," found nowhere else in Job; some Hebrew manuscripts read YHWH. The saying is the motto of Israel's wisdom books in another form: "the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge" (Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 9:10; Psalm 111:10). "Keep away from evil" uses the very words of 1:1 and 1:8, which describe Job as one who "kept away from evil." The end of the poem thus describes Job himself.
orig: יִרְאַת אֲדֹנָי הִיא חָכְמָה (yir'at Adonai hi chokhmah)
r: 1:1; 1:8; 2:3; Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 3:7; Proverbs 9:10; Psalm 111:10; Ecclesiastes 12:13; Sirach 1:14

a: And he said to humankind
p: Some think the last verse was added to make the poem say what Proverbs says. Others think it is its true climax.
b: The poem says wisdom is hidden from all living things (28:21). Then 28:28 gives humans a practical wisdom after all: fear God and shun evil. Many critics see a shift: the hidden cosmic wisdom known only to God (28:23–27) versus the moral wisdom offered to humans (28:28), and some judge the verse a later addition (it also breaks the meter). Others say that is the point: humans cannot grasp God's wisdom, but they can live in reverence and goodness, as Job did (1:1).

a: Job took up his poem again and said:
p: Chapters 29–31 form one long speech, Job's final statement before the court: past honor, present shame, oath.
b: Most scholars treat chapters 29–31 as a unit, Job's closing argument. In chapter 29 he remembers his former life, honored in the town gate as a judge and protector of the poor. In chapter 30 he describes his present humiliation. In chapter 31 he swears an oath of innocence and signs it (31:35). The speech is addressed partly to God (30:20–23), partly to anyone who will hear. Westermann compared its form to the lament psalms: a look back, a complaint, a plea of innocence. After it, "Job's words come to an end" (31:40).

a: when his lamp was shining above my head
p: A lamp above the head is a picture of God's favor and guidance, the opposite of Bildad's lamp that goes out.
b: Bildad said the lamp of the wicked goes out (18:5–6), and Job himself asked how often that really happens (21:17). Here Job remembers when God's lamp shone over him. The image is common in the Psalms: God lights the psalmist's lamp (Psalm 18:28); God's word is a lamp to the feet (Psalm 119:105). In a dark house, the lamp hung from the roof meant life and safety.

a: as I was in my harvest days
p: Literally "the days of my autumn." In Hebrew, autumn is the harvest season, so the phrase means the prime of life.
b: Choref is the season of autumn harvest and early rains in the Israelite calendar, the time of plenty, not of decline. So "my autumn" means Job's ripe years, his best time. English "autumn of life" means old age, which is why the Plain says "harvest days." "God's close friendship" renders sod, the inner circle of trusted counsel, used of God's friendship with the upright (Psalm 25:14; Proverbs 3:32) and of the heavenly council (15:8; Jeremiah 23:18).
orig: בִּימֵי חָרְפִּי (bime chorpi), "in the days of my autumn"

a: When I left home for the gate above the town
p: The gate was the town's court, market and meeting place. Job sat there as an elder and judge.
b: In Israelite towns the gate complex had benches where elders heard cases, as Boaz convenes the elders in the gate (Ruth 4:1–11) and Absalom courts the people there (2 Samuel 15:2). The "square" was the open space inside the gate. Archaeologists have uncovered such gates with benches at Dan, Gezer and other sites. Job was not just rich; he was a leading judge, which is why his honor and his concern for the poor (29:12–17) belong together. In chapter 31 he will swear he never used his "backing in the gate" against the fatherless (31:21).
r: Ruth 4:1–11; Deuteronomy 21:19; Deuteronomy 25:7; 2 Samuel 15:2; Amos 5:12; Amos 5:15; 31:21

a: and put a hand over their mouths
p: Leaders put their hands over their mouths in respect for Job. In the end Job does the same before God (40:4).
b: Putting a hand on the mouth is a gesture of silence before someone greater (21:5; Judges 18:19; Micah 7:16). In Job's glory days, nobles fell silent before him. After God speaks from the storm, Job says, "I lay a hand across my mouth" (40:4). The book turns the gesture of human honor into the gesture of a creature before its Creator.

a: for when the poor cried out, I came to their rescue
p: Eliphaz accused Job of neglecting widows and the fatherless (22:6–9). Job answers with his record.
b: Point by point, 29:12–17 reverses the charges of 22:6–9: Eliphaz said Job sent widows away and crushed the fatherless; Job says he rescued the fatherless and made the widow's heart sing. His list matches the duties of a just king in the ancient Near East and in Israel (Psalm 72:12–14; Jeremiah 22:15–16). Hammurabi's law code says in its epilogue that he set up his laws so that the strong would not wrong the weak and so that the orphan and the widow would get justice. Job claims to have lived out that ideal in his town.

a: I put on righteousness, and it put me on
p: The verb works both ways: Job wore righteousness, and righteousness wore him, the way the Spirit "put on" Gideon.
b: The Hebrew vayyilbasheni means "and it clothed itself with me." The same idiom says the Spirit of the LORD "clothed itself with" Gideon (Judges 6:34) and Amasai (1 Chronicles 12:18). So Job's justice was not a robe he put on and took off; it filled him. Clothing as a picture of character runs through the Bible: the Messiah wears righteousness as a belt (Isaiah 11:5), God puts on righteousness as armor (Isaiah 59:17), and believers "put on" Christ (Galatians 3:27; Ephesians 6:14). The "turban" (tsanif) was the headdress of a person of rank (Isaiah 62:3; Zechariah 3:5).
r: Judges 6:34; 1 Chronicles 12:18; Isaiah 11:5; Isaiah 59:17; Isaiah 61:10; Psalm 132:9; Ephesians 6:14

a: To the blind I was eyes
p: Job's care for the blind and lame matches Israel's law, which forbade tripping the blind and cursing the deaf.
b: Leviticus says, "Do not curse a deaf person, and do not set something to trip over in front of a blind person. Fear your God. I am the LORD" (Leviticus 19:14). Deuteronomy curses anyone "who sends a blind person the wrong way on the road" (Deuteronomy 27:18). Job goes beyond not harming: he guided the blind and carried the lame. In the Gospels, giving sight to the blind and making the lame walk are signs of the kingdom (Matthew 11:5; Isaiah 35:5–6).

a: Along with my nest I will breathe my last
p: Literally "with my nest I will expire." Job pictured an old bird ending its days at home; the rabbis heard the phoenix.
b: The Hebrew im-qinni egva' is "with (or in) my nest I will expire." Job expected to die in old age among his own household, his nest. The rabbis heard more. They read chol in the next line as the phoenix, a bird that dies in its nest and is renewed (Genesis Rabbah 19:5; Talmud Sanhedrin 108b), and "with my nest" fits that legend. The Greek's "palm tree" (phoinix, also the Greek word for the phoenix) may be a trace of the same idea. The variant panel sets out the three readings of the second line.

a: My root is open to the water
p: Job pictured himself as a well-watered tree, the image of the righteous in Psalm 1 and Jeremiah 17.
b: In Psalm 1:3 the righteous person is a tree set beside streams of water, and Jeremiah 17:8 says the one who trusts the LORD sends out roots by the stream and does not fear the heat. Job believed that picture about himself. Bildad used the opposite image: the roots of the wicked dry up below and their branches wither (18:16). The dew that rests all night is a sign of blessing (Genesis 27:28; Hosea 14:5).

a: as for the spring showers
p: Malqosh is the spring rain of March and April that fills out the grain before harvest.
b: Israel's rainy season begins with the early rains in autumn (yoreh) and ends with the late rains in spring (malqosh). If the late rains failed, the harvest failed (Deuteronomy 11:14; Jeremiah 3:3; Joel 2:23; James 5:7). People waited for Job's words like farmers watching the sky in spring. Deuteronomy uses the same picture for Moses' teaching falling like rain and dew (Deuteronomy 32:2).

a: I laughed with them, and they would not believe it
p: The Hebrew can mean Job's smile cheered the discouraged, or that people could not believe he smiled on them.
b: Literally: "I laughed at them, they did not believe, and the light of my face they did not cause to fall." One reading: when they lost heart, Job smiled on them, and they did not let his cheerful face go (or did not darken it). Another: they could hardly believe Job would smile on them, such was his rank. "The light of the face" is favor, as in the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:25) and Proverbs 16:15, where a king's shining face means life.
orig: אֶשְׂחַק אֲלֵהֶם לֹא יַאֲמִינוּ (esachaq alehem lo ya'aminu)

a: like someone who brings the mourners comfort
p: Job ends his memory of honor as a true comforter of mourners. His friends came to comfort him and failed.
b: The friends came to "shake their heads with him and comfort him" (2:11), but Job called them "comforters who bring trouble" (16:2) and their comfort empty (21:34). Here Job remembers being the one who comforted the grieving. Some scholars think the last line is a later addition because it breaks the picture of a king among troops. Others see it as the point of the whole chapter: Job's rank was used for others. A Christian reading notes Paul's picture of the God of all comfort, who comforts us so that we can comfort others (2 Corinthians 1:3–4).

a: And now they make fun of me
p: "And now" begins three sections of the chapter (30:1, 9, 16). Each drives the contrast with chapter 29.
b: Chapter 29 looked back; chapter 30 looks at now. The young men who once stepped aside for Job (29:8) now laugh at him, and they are the sons of men he thought too low to rank with his sheepdogs. The verb ma'as is "reject, despise": Job would have scorned their fathers. Job's contempt for these outcasts (30:1–8) troubles many readers, since in 24:4–12 he pitied the desert poor. Some think the outcasts are a different group, a lawless rabble rather than the oppressed poor. Others see Job's honest bitterness: humiliation by the lowest is the sharpest humiliation of all. Psalm 69:12 and Lamentations 3:14 describe the same mocking songs.

a: in the gloom of waste and ruin
p: The rare word emesh usually means "last night" or "yesterday." Here it may mean the gloom of the wasteland.
b: Emesh means "yesterday evening" in Genesis 31:29, 42 and 2 Kings 9:26. In this verse it seems to describe the desert itself: "the night (or gloom) of waste and desolation." Others read it as "they flee to the land that was waste of old," taking the verb 'oreq as "flee" (as in Arabic and Aramaic) rather than "gnaw." The Greek reads "those fleeing a waterless place, yesterday distress and misery." The sense is clear even if the details are not: the outcasts live on the edge of starvation.

a: broom roots are their bread
p: Orache (saltbush) is a salty desert shrub that the poor could eat. Broom roots are bitter, and may have been burned for warmth.
b: Malluach, from melach, "salt," is the saltbush or orache (Atriplex), whose sour leaves were eaten by the very poor; the Greek reads halima, the same plant. The broom (rotem) is the desert bush that Elijah slept under (1 Kings 19:4). Its roots are bitter and were used to make charcoal (Psalm 120:4). Some therefore read lachmam, "their bread," as lechummam, "to warm them." Either way, these are people who live on what no one else would touch.

a: so they throw off the bridle in front of me
p: Once God has weakened Job, the mockers drop all restraint, like animals that shake off the bridle.
b: Resen is a bridle or halter (Psalm 32:9; Isaiah 30:28). The mockers "send it away" in Job's presence: no respect holds them back any more. The first line gives the reason. God has slackened Job's cord, perhaps his bowstring (contrast 29:20, "the bow in my hand will keep its spring"), perhaps the cord of his tent, an image of life in 4:21. The Plain follows the Qere, the Masoretic reading tradition, "my cord"; the written consonants (Ketiv) have "his cord." See the variant panel and the Ketiv and Qere topic.

a: like the neck of my shirt, he wraps me tight
p: Job's tunic binds him at the neck. Whether from disease or from God's grip, he feels choked.
b: The second line reads literally "like the mouth of my tunic he girds me." The "mouth" of a garment is its neck opening (Exodus 28:32; compare Psalm 133:2). "He" is most likely God, as in 30:19, though the Hebrew may mean the garment itself. Either Job's wasted or swollen body no longer fits his clothes, or God has seized him by the collar, as the Greek reads the first line (see the variant panel).

a: and I am no better than dust and ashes
p: The phrase appears only here, in Abraham's prayer, and in Job's last words (42:6).
b: Abraham called himself "dust and ashes" when he dared to bargain with God over Sodom (Genesis 18:27). Job uses the phrase here as a picture of humiliation: God has thrown him in the mud. In his final reply Job says he changes his mind "on dust and ashes" (42:6). Whether 42:6 means repenting in ashes, being comforted as a mortal, or retracting his lawsuit, the echo of 30:19 is part of the debate; see the note at 42:6.

a: I call out to you, and you give me no answer
p: For the first time in this closing speech, Job turns to God and says "you."
b: Chapters 29 and 30 have spoken about God; here Job addresses him (30:20–23), as he did in his earlier laments (7:12–21; 10:2–22; 13:20–28). His complaint is the one of Psalm 22:2: I cry and you do not answer. The second line, in the Masoretic Text, makes it worse: God does look at Job, but only looks. Some witnesses add "not"; see the variant panel.

a: with your strong hand you bear me a grudge
p: The verb satam means to hold a grudge, to treat as an enemy. It is close in sound and sense to satan, "accuser."
b: Satam is used of Esau, who "held a grudge" against Jacob (Genesis 27:41), and of Joseph's brothers' fear that he would (Genesis 50:15). Job used it in 16:9: God has torn him in his anger and "held a grudge." The related verb satan means "to accuse, oppose"; from it comes ha-satan, the Accuser of the prologue (1:6). Readers who know the prologue see the irony: Job blames God for the hostility that the Accuser began. Job does not know of the heavenly scene.

a: you dissolve me in the crashing storm
p: The storm wind carries Job off and melts him away.
b: Job pictures himself lifted on the wind like chaff and dissolved in the storm, the same storm wind that carries off the wicked in 27:20–21. The Plain reads the written consonants as teshu'ah, the crash of a storm, the word used for "the thunder from his pavilion" in 36:29; the reading tradition has tushiyyah, "success" (see the variant panel).

a: For I know it: to death you will bring me back
p: The verb is "return": God will send Job back to death, as Adam returns to the dust from which he came.
b: The Hebrew teshiveni is "you will return me." It recalls Genesis 3:19 and Job's own earlier words (1:21; 10:9). Death is the "meeting house" (bet mo'ed) of all the living, the appointed place where everyone gathers in the end. The phrase sounds like ohel mo'ed, the "tent of meeting" where Israel met God; here the meeting place is the grave.
orig: מָוֶת תְּשִׁיבֵנִי (mavet teshiveni); בֵּית מוֹעֵד (bet mo'ed)

a: Surely, from the rubble, a man stretches out his hand
t: One of the hardest verses in Job
p: The Hebrew is unclear. The Greek turns it into a wish to kill himself; the Plain follows the most common modern reading.
b: Word by word: "surely not on a heap of ruins does he send a hand, if in his disaster to them a cry." The most common modern reading: even a man in ruins stretches out his hand and cries for help, so why should Job not cry out? Others read: "surely no one strikes a ruined man who cries for help" (as God has done to Job). The Septuagint reads "if only I could lay hands on myself, or ask another to do this for me," a wish for death that the Hebrew does not clearly contain. Job longs for death several times (3:20–22; 6:8–9; 7:15) but never says he will take his own life.

a: Did I not weep for the man having a hard day?
p: Job's question answers Eliphaz again: Job did feel the pain of the poor, so why does no one feel his?
b: The verse looks back to chapter 29 and forward to chapter 31. Job had compassion, so he expected compassion (30:26). Paul's "weep along with those who weep" (Romans 12:15) names the same virtue. The sudden turn from complaint to self-defense in the middle of a lament is typical of the lament psalms, which mix protest, memory and claims of loyalty (Psalm 35:13–14; Psalm 44:17–22).

a: I go about in black, where no sun shines
t: Black with mourning or with disease?
p: Qoder means "dark, dirty," the word for mourners in soiled clothes. "No sun" may mean gloom, or not sunburned.
b: Qoder describes mourners going about unwashed and dark-clothed (Psalm 35:14; Psalm 38:6; Psalm 42:9). "Without sun" (belo chammah) is read two ways: "blackened, but not by the sun," so his dark skin comes from disease (30:30), or "in gloom, with no sunshine." The Plain keeps the picture of mourning in a sunless world. Standing in the assembly to cry for help is the action of a plaintiff in a public court.
orig: קֹדֵר הִלַּכְתִּי בְּלֹא חַמָּה (qoder hillakhti belo chammah)

a: Jackals are my brothers now
t: Jackals and ostriches, not dragons and owls
p: The KJV has "dragons" and "owls." The Hebrew words mean jackals and ostriches, animals of the desert ruins.
b: Tannim (jackals) looks like tannin (sea monster, dragon), and older translators confused them; the KJV's "dragons" is a mistranslation here. Benot ya'anah, "daughters of the ostrich," is the ostrich, known for its mournful cry (Micah 1:8). Both animals haunt ruined cities in the prophets (Isaiah 13:21–22; Isaiah 34:13). Job's cries sound like theirs, and his company is now the wild things of the waste. The Greek has "sirens" and "ostriches."

a: My harp is given over to mourning
p: The lyre and pipe that once played at feasts now play laments. Job's life has become a funeral song.
b: The kinnor (lyre) and ugav (flute or pipe) are the instruments of joy, named in 21:12, where Job said the wicked dance to them. Lamentations 5:15 says the same of Jerusalem: its dancing became mourning. The chapter ends without hope, and Job moves straight to his oath.

a: I cut a covenant with my eyes.
p: Chapter 31 is a self-curse: "If I did X, may Y happen to me." It is the Bible's fullest list of private sins.
b: In ancient courts an accused person with no witnesses could clear himself by an oath: "If I have done this, may God do so to me." The law of Moses uses such oaths when no one saw what happened (Exodus 22:10–11; Numbers 5:19–22). Job swears to about fourteen sins and calls curses on himself for each. Many of them are inward or hidden: a lustful look, trust in wealth, secret joy at an enemy's ruin, a kiss blown to the moon. Michael Dick has shown how the chapter follows the pattern of a legal oath meant to force the other side, God, to answer in court (31:35). Egyptian and Babylonian texts have similar lists; see the note at 31:5. The Old Greek lacked 31:1–4, so in it the oath began at 31:5; Origen supplied the opening from Theodotion (checked in NETS).

a: So how could I fix my gaze on a young girl?
p: Job swears he did not even look with desire. Jesus will teach that lust in the heart is adultery.
b: The law forbids adultery and craving a neighbor's wife: "You must not commit adultery" and "You must not crave your neighbor's wife" (Exodus 20:14; Exodus 20:17). Job's covenant goes further, to the eye itself. Jesus says whoever looks at a woman to desire her has already committed adultery in his heart (Matthew 5:28); Sirach 9:5 and 9:8 warn against gazing at a virgin or a beautiful woman. The betulah is a young unmarried woman. Some scholars think the word here is a hint at the goddess Anat, "the Virgin" of Ugarit, so that the sin is idolatry; most read it plainly.
r: Exodus 20:14; Exodus 20:17; Matthew 5:28; Sirach 9:5; Sirach 9:8; Proverbs 6:25; 2 Samuel 11:2

a: If I have kept company with falsehood
t: Lists of sins in Egypt and Babylon
p: Egypt's Book of the Dead and Babylon's Shurpu incantations list sins a person swears he never did.
b: In chapter 125 of the Egyptian Book of the Dead, the dead person stands before Osiris and the 42 judges and declares that he has done no wrong, has not robbed, has not killed, and has not taken milk from a child's mouth. This is often called the "negative confession." The Babylonian Shurpu tablets list sins a sick man may have committed unknowingly, such as moving a boundary or lying, so that the gods may release him. Job 31 shares the form, a list of denials in a judgment, and some of the content. The differences are real: Job speaks to the one God, not to a court of gods; he swears in life, not after death; and he challenges God to answer him.

a: let him set me on the scales of righteousness
p: Job asks to be weighed on true scales, the honest weights that Israel's law demanded in the market.
b: Leviticus commands, "Have scales that are right, weights that are right" (Leviticus 19:36), and Deuteronomy 25:13–16 forbids two kinds of weights. Job asks God to treat him as fairly as the law tells merchants to treat buyers. In Egyptian art, the heart of the dead was weighed on a scale against the feather of truth; Job's image may recall it, but weighing as a picture of judgment is common (Daniel 5:27; Proverbs 16:2).

a: or my heart has gone where my eyes led
p: Numbers warns Israel not to follow their hearts and eyes. Job swears he did not.
b: The tassels on Israelite clothing were to remind the wearer not to go after his own heart and eyes (Numbers 15:39). Job's "blot" (mum) on the hands is a defect or stain, the word used for blemishes that disqualify animals for sacrifice (Leviticus 22:20) and for priests (Leviticus 21:17). The curse that follows (31:8) is the farmer's curse of the covenant: to sow and have another eat (Leviticus 26:16; Deuteronomy 28:30–33).

a: If a woman has led my heart astray
p: The second oath is about adultery: lurking at a neighbor's door to sleep with his wife.
b: Here the sin is the act, not only the look (31:1). The law calls it a capital crime: "A man who commits adultery with another man's wife... must be put to death, the man and the woman who commit adultery" (Leviticus 20:10). Leviticus 18:20 forbids it as making oneself unclean. Proverbs 7 tells of a young man lured to a married woman's door at twilight. Job says he never lurked there (compare the adulterer waiting for dusk in 24:15).

a: then may my wife turn another man's millstone
p: The curse falls on Job's wife: may she grind for another man and be used by others. Modern readers find this hard.
b: Grinding grain at the hand mill was the work of slave women (Exodus 11:5; Isaiah 47:2); "grind for another" may also be a sexual euphemism, as rabbinic readers and many moderns take it, and "crouch over her" certainly is. The curse matches the crime, adultery for adultery, which is the logic of ancient law (eye for eye, Exodus 21:24). But it lays the penalty on a woman who did nothing. Commentators note honestly that the oath reflects a world in which a wife's body was counted as part of her husband's household and honor (compare 2 Samuel 12:11). The book does not comment.

a: That is a shameful outrage
t: Zimmah and a crime for judges
p: Zimmah is a word for gross sexual sin. "A crime for the judges" means one that human courts must punish.
b: Zimmah is used of incest and prostitution (Leviticus 18:17; Leviticus 19:29; Judges 20:6). "A crime for the judges" ('avon pelilim) marks adultery as a public offense, not only a private one, for Israel's courts to try (Deuteronomy 22:22). Job places some sins before human judges (31:11, 28) and all of them before God (31:14, 23). He adds that adultery is "a fire that eats down to Abaddon," as Proverbs warns that adultery is fire in the lap (Proverbs 6:27–29).

a: If I waved away the case of my slave or my slave woman
p: Job says he heard his slaves' complaints. The law protected slaves from abuse, but Job grounds their rights in creation.
b: The Hebrew eved can mean "servant" or "slave"; here the household slave is meant (the site's term list renders eved by context). The law limited a master's power: a slave who lost an eye or tooth went free (Exodus 21:26–27), a master who killed a slave was punished (Exodus 21:20), and slaves rested on the Sabbath (Exodus 20:10; Deuteronomy 5:14). Leviticus 19:20 deals with a slave woman's case. But no law gives a slave the right to bring a complaint against his master. Job goes further than the law: he heard their cases himself, because God made both master and slave (31:15).
orig: עַבְדִּי וַאֲמָתִי (avdi va'amati), "my slave and my slave woman"
r: Exodus 21:20; Exodus 21:26–27; Exodus 20:10; Deuteronomy 5:14; Deuteronomy 15:12–15; Leviticus 25:39–43

a: Did not one Maker shape us both in the womb?
t: Master and slave made by one God
p: Job's reason is creation: the same God formed master and slave in the womb. Few ancient texts say this.
b: Ancient law codes treated slaves as property with fewer rights than the free. Job argues from a shared Maker that a slave is his equal before God. Malachi 2:10 makes a similar point, asking whether one God did not create us all, and Proverbs 14:31 and Proverbs 22:2 say that rich and poor have the same Maker. Paul tells masters they and their slaves have the same Master in heaven (Ephesians 6:9; Colossians 4:1). Gregory of Nyssa, in the 300s, used such reasoning in one of the first Christian attacks on slavery itself. See the image of God topic.
r: Malachi 2:10; Proverbs 14:31; Proverbs 22:2; Ephesians 6:9; Colossians 4:1; Galatians 3:28; 10:8–12; Psalm 139:13

a: If I have kept from the poor what they longed for
t: The poor, the widow and the fatherless
p: Job's next oaths (31:16–23) answer Eliphaz's charges in 22:6–9 one by one, and match the laws for the poor.
b: Eliphaz said Job withheld bread from the hungry and sent widows away; Job swears he shared his bread with the fatherless, raised the widow's son as a father, and clothed the naked with his sheep's wool. The law commands, "Do not bend the justice due a foreigner or a fatherless child, and do not take a widow's garment as a pledge" (Deuteronomy 24:17), and leaves the forgotten sheaf "for the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow" (Deuteronomy 24:19). Deuteronomy 15:7–11 commands an open hand to the needy. Job's claim is that he did not only obey such laws; he lived their spirit.
r: 22:6–9; Deuteronomy 24:17; Deuteronomy 24:19–21; Deuteronomy 15:7–11; Exodus 22:22–24; Isaiah 58:7; Matthew 25:35–36

a: for since I was young he has grown up with me as if I were his father
p: Job cared for the fatherless as a father and guided the widow "from my mother's womb," meaning all his life.
b: The verse is a parenthesis. The Hebrew is literally "from my youth he grew up with me as a father, and from my mother's womb I guided her." "He" is the fatherless child of 31:17, and "her" the widow of 31:16. Some repoint the first verb to read "he (God) raised me like a father," so that Job learned compassion from God. "From my mother's womb" is a figure for "as long as I have lived" (compare Psalm 22:10; Psalm 71:6).
orig: כִּי מִנְּעוּרַי גְּדֵלַנִי כְאָב (ki mine'urai gedelani kh'av)

a: if his loins did not bless me
p: The warm, clothed body of the poor man thanked Job. The Hebrew says his loins (his waist) blessed him.
b: The poor man's body, wrapped in wool from Job's sheep, "blessed" Job, as if the warmth itself were his thanks. The law says a lender must return a poor man's coat at night "so that he can sleep in his coat and bless you" (Deuteronomy 24:13), and Exodus asks of the poor man's coat, "What will he sleep in?" (Exodus 22:27). Job's line sounds like an answer to those laws. The Ketiv and Qere differ in number, "his loin" and "his loins," with no change in sense.

a: because I saw I had backing in the gate
p: Job swears he never used his influence in the town court to crush the fatherless.
b: As a leading elder (29:7), Job could have won any case. The law warns judges: "Do not take a bribe, for a bribe blinds those who see clearly" (Exodus 23:8), "Do no wrong in judgment" (Leviticus 19:15), and "Do not push aside the right of the needy among you when his case is heard" (Exodus 23:6). Waving the hand (henif yad) is a threatening gesture, perhaps a vote in court or a raised fist. The curse fits the crime: may the arm that was raised be torn off (31:22).

a: If I have leaned on gold for my confidence
p: Job swears he never trusted his riches, the sin that Eliphaz hinted at (22:24–25).
