b: Job was the richest man in the East (1:3), yet he says gold was never his security. Psalm 49:6–7 and Psalm 62:10 warn against trusting riches, and Jesus' parable of the rich fool makes the same point (Luke 12:16–21). Paul calls greed "idolatry" (Colossians 3:5), and Job sets the oath about gold right before the oath about worshiping the sun and moon (31:26–28), as if he saw the two as related. When Job lost everything, he said, "The LORD gave, and the LORD took" (1:21).
r: 1:3; 1:21; 22:24–25; Psalm 49:6–7; Psalm 52:7; Psalm 62:10; Proverbs 11:28; Luke 12:16–21; Colossians 3:5; 1 Timothy 6:17

a: if I watched the light as it blazed
p: "The light" is the sun. Throwing a kiss to the sun or moon was an act of worship in the ancient Near East.
b: Sun and moon were among the great gods of Job's world: Shamash and Sin in Mesopotamia (the moon god had famous temples at Ur and Harran), Ra in Egypt. A worshiper might kiss his own hand and raise it toward the god, as kissing an idol was a mark of worship (1 Kings 19:18; Hosea 13:2). Deuteronomy warns, "when you raise your eyes to the sky and see the sun, the moon and the stars... do not be pulled away to bow down to them and serve them" (Deuteronomy 4:19), and makes such worship a capital crime (Deuteronomy 17:3–5). Job swears that even in his heart, in secret, he was never tempted.
r: Deuteronomy 4:19; Deuteronomy 17:3–5; 2 Kings 23:5; Jeremiah 8:2; Ezekiel 8:16; 1 Kings 19:18; Hosea 13:2

a: since I would have denied the God above
p: Worship of the sun would deny the one God. It is the only oath in the chapter about worship itself.
b: The verb kichesh means "to deny, to lie to, to act falsely toward." To worship the sun would be to lie to God, the God "above" the sun and moon. The first commandment is behind it: "You must not have any other gods in my presence" (Exodus 20:3), and Exodus 22:20 puts anyone who sacrifices to other gods under the ban. Job is not an Israelite and never mentions the covenant, but his oath matches the first commandment as well as the last.

a: If I was glad when someone who hated me was ruined
t: No joy at an enemy's fall
p: Job swears he never gloated over his enemy or cursed him. This is among the most inward of his oaths.
b: Proverbs warns against being glad when your enemy falls (Proverbs 24:17). The law commands returning an enemy's straying ox or donkey: "If you meet your enemy's ox or his donkey straying, you must bring it back to him" (Exodus 23:4–5), and Leviticus 19:17–18 forbids hatred in the heart and grudges. Job's oath reaches the hidden feelings those laws aim at. Jesus' "love your enemies" goes one step further still (Matthew 5:43–44). The verse that follows (31:30) interrupts the "if" to insist: I did not even let my mouth curse him.
r: Proverbs 24:17–18; Proverbs 25:21–22; Exodus 23:4–5; Leviticus 19:17–18; Matthew 5:43–44; Romans 12:14–20

a: 'Show us anyone who has not eaten his fill of his meat!'
p: Job's household boasted that everyone had eaten Job's meat. The Hebrew could also be read as something darker.
b: Most commentators read the line as a proverb of hospitality: Job's household would say, "Who has not had his fill of Job's meat?" so generous was his table. The KJV's wording ("Oh that we had of his flesh!") can be taken as the servants' wish to get at Job himself. Marvin Pope (Anchor Bible) saw in the line a hint of sexual abuse of guests, which Job would be denying. The hospitality reading fits 31:32, the foreigner who never slept in the street.
orig: מִי־יִתֵּן מִבְּשָׂרוֹ לֹא נִשְׂבָּע (mi-yitten mibbesaro lo nisba')

a: Out in the street no foreigner passed the night
p: Job welcomed travelers. Israel's law commands care for the foreigner because Israel itself had been foreign in Egypt.
b: Ger is the foreigner living away from his own people. Exodus commands, "Do not mistreat a foreigner living among you, and do not press him hard, for you were foreigners living in the land of Egypt" (Exodus 22:21), and Leviticus says, "You are to love him as yourself, because you were foreigners in the land of Egypt" (Leviticus 19:34). The town that let a traveler sleep in its square was disgraced (Judges 19:15–20). "To the road" (la'orach) may be read, with different vowels, as "to the traveler" (la'oreach).
r: Exodus 22:21; Exodus 23:9; Leviticus 19:33–34; Deuteronomy 10:19; Judges 19:15–20; Hebrews 13:2

a: if I have hidden my wrongs as Adam did
p: Ke'adam can mean "like Adam," who hid after his sin, or simply "as humans do."
b: Adam is both the first man's name and the common word for "human." Read as a name, the verse recalls Genesis 3:8–10: Adam hid among the trees and blamed the woman. Read as a common noun, it means "as people usually do." Both readings are old; the Targum and many Christian interpreters favor Adam, while many moderns prefer "as others do" (compare Hosea 6:7, with the same ambiguity). Either way, Job swears he did not cover his sins for fear of public shame (31:34). Proverbs 28:13 says that whoever hides his sins will not prosper.

a: Here is my mark
p: The "mark" is the Hebrew letter tav, the last letter of the alphabet, which in the old script was shaped like an X.
b: Tav in the old Hebrew script looked like an X or a cross, and could serve as a signature (compare Ezekiel 9:4, where a tav is marked on foreheads). Job signs his written oath and demands that his "opponent at law" (ish rivi, "the man of my lawsuit") write out the charges in a document (sefer). He means God. It is a summons: Job has done all he can, and now God must answer or acquit him. God does answer, from the storm (38:1), but not with charges.

a: I would hoist it onto my shoulder
p: Job would carry the indictment proudly, sure it would prove his innocence.
b: The document is the charge written by Job's accuser (31:35). Far from hiding it, Job would wear it on his shoulder like a badge of office (compare Isaiah 9:6; Isaiah 22:22) and wrap it round his head like a crown. He is that sure no charge will stand. He would then walk up to God "like a prince" (nagid, a leader) and give a full account of every step (31:37), the opposite of Adam hiding among the trees (31:33).

a: If the soil I farm has cried out over me
t: A last oath out of place?
p: After the signature, Job adds one more oath. Many scholars think 31:38–40 once stood earlier in the chapter.
b: The climax of the oath seems to be 31:35–37, with Job's signature and challenge. Then come three more verses of "if," about the land. Many scholars move 31:38–40b to follow 31:8, 31:25 or 31:34, and some translations print them there. Others defend the order: the oath ends where Job's life began, with the soil, and the land itself, like the blood of Abel (Genesis 4:10), is called as a witness. The Plain keeps the Hebrew order.

a: if I have eaten what it grew and paid no money for it
p: Job swears he never seized land or worked its owners to death. It recalls Ahab and Naboth's vineyard.
b: "Its owners" (be'aleha) may be the original owners of the land, or the laborers who worked it. To "squeeze the breath out" of them is to work them to death or to kill them for their land, as Jezebel had Naboth killed so Ahab could take his vineyard (1 Kings 21). The prophets condemn those who add house to house and covet fields (Isaiah 5:8; Micah 2:2). The law says the wages of a hired worker must not stay overnight (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14–15). The curse is fitting: thorns instead of wheat, the curse of Eden's ground (Genesis 3:17–18).
r: 1 Kings 21:1–19; Isaiah 5:8; Micah 2:2; Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14–15; Genesis 3:17–18; James 5:4

a: Here Job's words come to an end.
p: A scribe's note ends Job's speeches, like the note at the end of David's prayers in Psalm 72:20.
b: The Hebrew tammu divre Iyyov, "the words of Job are complete," is a closing note like the one that ends the prayers of David son of Jesse (Psalm 72:20). It marks the end of the debate. Job does speak again, but only two short replies to God (40:3–5; 42:1–6). The verb tamam is related to tam, "wholehearted" (1:1), and some readers hear a play on it: Job's words are complete, like Job himself. Elihu now steps in (32:1–5).

a: reeking weeds
p: Bo'shah is a weed with a bad smell, from the verb "to stink." Its kind is unknown.
b: The word comes from ba'ash, "to stink." Isaiah 5:2, 4 uses a related word for the "wild grapes" or rotten grapes of God's vineyard. The KJV's "cockle" names a European weed. Thorns and foul weeds where grain should grow is the curse on the ground after Eden (Genesis 3:18).

a: It is veiled from the eyes of all that lives
t: A shorter poem in the Old Greek
p: The Old Greek lacked about a third of this poem. Origen filled the gaps from Theodotion and marked them.
b: The lines that Origen marked as missing from the Old Greek include, roughly, 28:3–4, much of 28:5–9, the list of treasures in 28:14–19, 28:21–22 and 28:26–27 (checked in the NETS translation, which prints them in brackets; Gentry studies these lines in detail). The Greek translator of Job often shortened repetitive poetry, so most scholars take the gaps as his cuts rather than as evidence of a shorter Hebrew poem. The Hebrew of the whole poem is also attested in part by the Qumran Targum, whose columns cover 28:4–13 and 28:20–28 in the Hebrew order (Zuckerman and Reed). Still, the Old Greek reader met a briefer poem, with fewer mining scenes and treasures and without the voices of Abaddon and Death.

a: what could I do when God stood up?
t: The oldest Hebrew copies of the oath
p: Two Dead Sea Scroll fragments, from about 175–60 BC and 50–1 BC, preserve parts of 31:14–21.
b: 4Q99 (4QJob-a), dated about 175–60 BC, preserves pieces of 31:14–19, and 4Q100 (4QJob-b), dated about 50–1 BC, preserves pieces of 31:20–21. They are among the oldest Hebrew copies of Job. The English edition of the scrolls reports one difference from the Masoretic Text in these verses, a different word order in 31:15, and none in 31:20–21. These details were checked in the Dead Sea Scrolls Bible Translations pages for 4Q99 and 4Q100, not in the official edition (DJD 16). As far as they go, the fragments show the oath in substantially its Masoretic wording two centuries before Christ.
